sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Hokkaidō** (*hokkaido*) — The Northern Road — belongs to the Japanese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Northern Island". The name means "Northern sea circuit"[^1].

Hokkaidō is Japan's youngest name on its oldest ground: an island inhabited for twenty thousand years, homeland of the Ainu, mapped into the Japanese state only in 1869 — a frontier whose ancient name, Ainu Mosir, still names the deeper country beneath the modern one.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Hokkaidō** and serves its temple at [hokkaidō.com](https://xn--hokkaid-cmb.com). The restoration preserves the long vowel ō — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses — which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *hokkaido* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, 712.
Nihon Shoki (Chronicles of Japan), Translated by W. G. Aston (excerpts), 720.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Japanese characters as **北海道**. Etymologically it means "Northern sea circuit"[^1].

The ASCII form *hokkaido* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Hokkaidō** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves the long vowel ō — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses — which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **h** → **H** — Same
- **o** → **o** — Short vowel
- **k** → **k** — Same
- **k** → **k** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same
- **d** → **d** — Same
- **o** → **ō** — Macron: long vowel

The project holds the domain **hokkaidō.com** (xn--hokkaid-cmb.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki (Chronicles of Japan), Translated by W. G. Aston (excerpts), 720.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/hok.kai.doː/** — Japanese (Hepburn).[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: hok-KAI-doh, with the long final ō.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Japanese** — 北海道
- **Ainu** — Ainu Mosir
- **Older name** — Ezochi
- **Owned form** — Hokkaidō

Hokkaidō 北海道 — "North Sea Road" — carries a long final ō, the doubled vowel the macron preserves. The name dates only from 1869, when the explorer Matsuura Takeshirō proposed it for the island the Ainu long called Ainu Mosir, "the quiet land of humans." The long ō of dō is a doubled vowel in kana (どう); the macron is the romanization of that extra beat.

sources.citation: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, 712.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name is written in Japanese characters as **北海道**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *hokkaido* and the PuniCodex restoration **Hokkaidō** are measured: the restoration preserves its vowel quantity of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.[^1]

Written 北海道: north, sea, road — the three kanji of the Meiji-era name. The older indigenous toponymy is Ainu: Ainu Mosir ("land of the humans"), and the island's pre-modern Japanese name Ezochi ("land of the Ezo") survives in the history books the new name replaced.

sources.citation: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, 712.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Hokkaidō is Japan's youngest name on its oldest ground: an island inhabited for twenty thousand years, homeland of the Ainu, mapped into the Japanese state only in 1869 — a frontier whose ancient name, Ainu Mosir, still names the deeper country beneath the modern one.[^1]

### The Snow Country

Drift ice, powder snow, and the Sapporo Snow Festival — the island's signature climate.

### Ainu Mosir

"The quiet land of humans" — the Ainu name for the island, older than any map of Japan.

### The Kaitakushi

The Colonization Commission of 1869: the frontier office that made Ezochi into Hokkaidō.

### Shiretoko

The peninsula UNESCO calls one of the world's richest temperate ecosystems — Ainu for "the end of the land."

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki (Chronicles of Japan), Translated by W. G. Aston (excerpts), 720.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Hokkaidō concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The bear** — Kim-un-kamuy, the mountain god of the Ainu — honoured in the iomante ceremony
- **The drift ice** — The winter sea that feeds the whole food chain of the north
- **The lavender field** — Furano's summer signature — the cultivated frontier in bloom

sources.citation: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, 712.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Hokkaidō's mythology is Ainu: a kamuy-cosmos where every animal, fire, and tool has a spirit-owner, and where the human world is maintained by right exchange with the unseen.[^1]

### Ainu Mosir and Kamuy Mosir (The Land)

Ainu oral tradition divides existence between Ainu Mosir, the land of humans, and Kamuy Mosir, the land of the spirits — and teaches that kamuy visit the human world wearing animal bodies as gifts. The bear is the mountain god's greatest visitation; the fire goddess, Ape-huci-kamuy, keeps every hearth and carries every prayer to the spirit world. The island itself is a borderland between the two realms.[^2]

### Iomante (The Ceremony)

The iomante — "sending off" — returns the visiting bear-spirit to Kamuy Mosir with songs, prayers, and gifts, so that the god will tell the other kamuy of human courtesy and come again in generous flesh. Long misread by outsiders as cruelty, it is among the most studied hunting ceremonies on earth: a theology of gratitude in which killing and honouring are the same act.

### From Ezochi to Hokkaidō (The Frontier)

The island's modern foundation-myth is documentary: in 1869 the new Meiji state renamed Ezochi, established the Kaitakushi (Colonization Commission), and invited American advisers — Capron, Clark ("Boys, be ambitious!") — to lay out farms, ports, and Sapporo itself on the American grid. A century of settlement followed; the Ainu were legally recognized as indigenous only in 2008, and the Ainu Promotion Act of 2019 opened a new chapter at last.

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki (Chronicles of Japan), Translated by W. G. Aston (excerpts), 720.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Ainu religion absorbed and resisted Japanese and Russian pressure in equal measure: Orthodox missions among the Kuril Ainu, Buddhist temples on the coasts, and the yukar epics — sung in an isolate language with no close relatives — keeping the older world intact in verse. The twentieth century added a third strand: the Ainu cultural revival, led by figures like the poet and legislator Kayano Shigeru, made the island's first culture a national conversation.[^1]

Within the Japanese tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[fujin|Fūjin]], [[honshu|Honshū]], [[jizo|Jizō]], [[kobe|Kōbe]], [[kyoto|Kyōto]], and [[kyushu|Kyūshū]].

sources.citation: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, 712.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Hokkaidō supplies a third of Japan's food from a tenth of its land; Sapporo beer, the Snow Festival's ice palaces, and the lavender of Furano are national brands. The 2020 opening of Upopoy, the National Ainu Museum and Park at Shiraoi, gave the island's first people their first national institution. In the history of colonialism, the Kaitakushi is studied worldwide as Japan's own frontier — the laboratory where it practiced the modernization it later exported.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, 712.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: Hokkaidō holds some of the world's oldest pottery: Jōmon-period cord-marked vessels from sites like Taishō date beyond 14,000 years, among the earliest ceramic traditions on earth. The Shiretoko peninsula is a UNESCO World Heritage site for its marine-terrestrial food web; the Oshoro stone circles and the Ofuna shell middens mark the island's deep ritual past. Hakodate's Goryōkaku — the star fort of the last Tokugawa loyalists (1869) — is where the old Japan made its final stand on the new island.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, 712.

sections.label: Kojiki & Nihon Shoki
sections.body:
The island's names record its double history.

- **Ainu Mosir** — 'the quiet land of humans'; the Ainu name, older than Japan's maps.
- **Ezochi (蝦夷地)** — 'land of the Ezo'; the pre-modern Japanese name the Meiji state replaced.
- **Hokkaidō (北海道)** — 'the North Sea Road'; Matsuura Takeshirō's coinage of 1869.
- **Kita no kuni** — 'the northern country'; the vernacular poetry-name.
- **Wajinchi no soto** — 'beyond the Japanese land'; the Edo-period formula that marked the frontier.

sources.citation: The Ainu toponymic studies (Kayano Shigeru); Hokkaido prefectural records.

sections.label: Shinto Sources
sections.body: The island's sacred geography is double. The Ainu kept no temples — their sanctuaries were the **kamuy-nomi sites**: bear-ceremony grounds, sacred fireplaces, and the ritual areas of the kotan villages, now studied at sites like Upopoy and the Akan Ainu Kotan. The Japanese state added its own: **Hokkaidō Jingū** in Sapporo (founded 1869 as the frontier's tutelary shrine), and the **Ise-style** pioneer shrines of the colonization era. Shiretoko — 'the end of the land' in Ainu — is the island's natural sanctuary, UNESCO-listed for the ecosystem the kamuy-cosmos named first.

sources.citation: The Upopoy/National Ainu Museum publications; Hokkaido Jingu records.

sections.label: Japanese Buddhist Sources
sections.body: Buddhism reached the island in the shadow of the state: Esoteric temples of the Matsumae era, the frontier chapels of the colonization period, and — most enduringly — the Ainu-Buddhist contact along the coasts, where the yukar's kamuy world met the dharma without merging. The island's modern Buddhist geography is the settlers': Sapporo's great temples, the Ōtani and Jōdo Shinshū missions that followed the farm families north, and the memorial temples of the Tohoku diaspora. The north kept its own question: whose spirits receive the sutras.

sources.citation: The Hokkaido temple records; studies of Ainu-Buddhist contact.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Hokkaidō is the island of two names — the one it was given and the one it had. It asks the frontier's hardest question, the one every settled map must answer: whose land was this before it was yours — and can the new name learn to carry the old one's meaning?

The island's two names have begun, at last, to speak to each other: the Ainu language taught in Upopoy's halls, the iomante explained rather than exoticized, the snow country marketed by its indigenous name's dignity. Frontiers are usually where names die; Hokkaidō is attempting the rarer thing — a map where the new name carries the old one's meaning. It is the experiment every settler society eventually must run, and the north island is running it in public.

And the snow keeps its own counsel over both names. Drift ice feeds the sea, the sea feeds the town, and the bear sleeps through the argument of maps — the kamuy-cosmos and the prefecture sharing one winter. The island's patience is its answer: the land outlasts every name it is given, and quietly teaches each new name what it means.

The drift ice still arrives each winter on schedule older than any name, feeding the bloom that feeds the sea — the island's oldest economy, unbranded. The Ainu ceremony sent the bear-spirit home with gifts so it would return; the modern island sends its food south with the same hope. Frontier or homeland, the north keeps its own account: what the land gives, the land can stop giving — and every name we call it is a promise to keep listening.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, 712.
